name: David Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel. The Panel has no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and our conversation is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day on the building site.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead carpenter on a two-storey school extension outside Greyburn, doing stairs, timber partitions and the odd roof repair. I get there before the van, compare the delivered timber with my measurements, then set the younger pair on the straight runs while I tackle the crooked stair corner. I've got a trade certificate and thirty years on tools, and I still like seeing a child-sized handrail fit properly. The contractor pays below the city rate, but there are only two other builders within a workable drive.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how much room is there in the budget?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lise works home-care shifts that move around from week to week, and our son is grown and living across town. We have roughly three weeks of bills saved after a roof leak, so I can't gamble our income on a shiny machine. I use AI every day to compare timber quantities and draft supplier questions, then check each number against the drawing and the stock on the van. I move quickly with a tool when it earns its keep, but it still gets measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a small planning shortcut is fine if it gets the right boards delivered. A phone still cannot tell me whether a stair stringer is twisted until I put a level on it. The school extension will need carpenters through the winter either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately the AI plateau does not settle the spring booking after the school job. Our savings cover around three weeks, and Lise's care rota varies, so a month without a site would be hard. I'm good at my trade, but local builders do not have a queue of openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the school stairs and ask the contractor for the next signed start date by February. I'd use my existing quantity tool only after checking the timber count against the delivered bundle. If two paid Saturdays come up, I'd put their net pay into a separate emergency reserve rather than buy another gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about the gap after the school, not frightened of the little AI change. I can manage an ordinary week, but I cannot stretch three weeks of money into a long spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if February brings no signed start date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask both nearby builders what they actually have booked and what hourly rate they pay. The city is too far for a casual day here and there once fuel is counted. I would take a firm paid offer, not leave the school site for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the quantity tool got a board count wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It counted the landing wall twice last month and asked for six extra boards. I found it when I compared the paper drawing with the pile beside the van. The supplier would have charged us and the boys would have spent the morning moving timber we did not need.

say: I would accept a **small planning shortcut** after checking the physical materials.
I would say the **school extension** still needs carpenters through winter.
think: The **unsigned spring booking** is my real worry in this mild future.
Three weeks saved and Lise’s **variable care rota** cannot cover a long site gap.
do: Finish the **school stairs** and ask for a signed next start date by February.
Save the net pay from **two available Saturdays** for an emergency reserve.
S0.quote: A phone still cannot tell me whether a stair stringer is twisted until I put a level on it.
fieldNote: His daily AI use is checked against **drawings and materials**, even in the mildest scenario.
The school contract is real; the **next spring start** is not, and three weeks of savings limit his patience.

steps.text: Finish school stairs and ask the contractor for a signed spring start
Save net pay from two available Saturday shifts in the emergency reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster orders are worth trying on one real stair run before they set targets for everybody. A planner can print twelve doors in an hour, but we still have to hang each one plumb. I'd want site workers paid to correct the drawing when it gets the old wall wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site work stays mostly hands-on while writing, buying and scheduling move first. That could make my quantity skill useful, or the contractor could use faster plans to cut a carpenter from the gang. Lise's care work needs hands, but a tighter booking system might make her shifts less predictable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pilot the approved ordering tool on the next two stair runs and record both the right quantities and the mistakes. I'd show the results at the crew meeting and ask for written paid checking time before the new targets start. If the contractor cuts my paid days for two rosters, I'd ask the nearby renovation firm for its posted lead rate and guaranteed hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though there's a useful part to it. I'd like fewer wasted timber deliveries, but I cannot pay the heating bill with an unpaid software trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair trial pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An hour to compare the AI list with the drawing and the delivered boards, plus the time to correct a wrong line. Last month a missed landing joist would have stopped us for half a day. I won't call a tool efficient if the crew absorbs the mistakes for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about the renovation job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the posted rate, travel distance and the number of guaranteed paid days before leaving the school extension. A nice title would not help if fuel eats the raise. I'd talk it through with Lise after two genuinely short rosters, not after one nervous Monday.

say: I would **trial faster ordering** on real stair runs with a paid check.
I would ask managers to count the time crews spend correcting **wrong lists**.
think: My **physical carpentry** should last while site buying and schedules change first.
Faster plans could still **cut paid days**, and Lise’s care rota may become less predictable.
do: Pilot approved **ordering software** on two stair runs and record its errors.
Ask for written **paid checking time** before targets change.
Seek a **posted lead vacancy** after two short rosters only if its pay and travel work.
feel: **Anxious**, with some hope of fewer wasted deliveries.
S1.quote: I cannot pay the heating bill with an unpaid software trial.
fieldNote: He sees real value in fewer wasted **timber deliveries**, but asks who pays to catch mistakes.
A change-job trigger is **two short rosters** and an adequate posted rate after travel costs.

steps.text: Pilot approved ordering software on two stair runs and log errors
Ask the contractor for written paid checking time before new targets
Seek a posted bill-covering lead role after two short rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI arrives by 2028 and may take buying and drawings first. A robot able to fit stairs like us follows around 2031, so the hand work has a short window, not a lifelong shield. The contractor should say plainly how many paid people the new setup needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daily AI habit may help me check a first pilot, but it doesn't make a robot job appear. By 2031 a machine could cut the stair work I've earned my living from for thirty years. Three weeks of savings and variable care wages would not carry us through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the contractor this month for written 2028 purchasing and 2031 robot staffing plans, including the paid safety checker. I'd keep taking available school shifts and put any extra net Saturday pay into the emergency reserve. I'd enrol in a local controls course only if a funded place, paid study time and a posted job with bill-covering pay are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed by the speed. I can learn a machine, but I cannot make a wage or a training place appear by wanting one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the course has no confirmed funding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep earning on the school site and ask the provider to put the fee and study hours in writing. If the course costs more than our three-week reserve, I do not sign up. I would ask whether any local builder has actually posted a controls role at a wage that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks a stair after the robot fits it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone must measure the rise and make sure a child does not trip on it. I'd take that job only with paid authority to stop a faulty installation and a posted contract. Calling me a safety expert while leaving the check unpaid is not a job.

say: I would ask how many **paid site roles** remain after thinking AI and robots.
I would require a **real safety checker** beside robot-built stairs.
think: A robot could cut my **stair-fitting wage** around 2031 despite my daily AI use.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot bridge a long job search.
do: Request written **2028 and 2031 staffing** and paid safety duties.
Keep available **paid school shifts** and save extra net Saturday wages.
Enrol in **local controls training** only with funding, paid time and a posted bill-covering role.
S2.quote: My daily AI habit may help me check a first pilot, but it doesn't make a robot job appear.
fieldNote: His confidence with AI does not create a **paid robot vacancy**.
He names three gates for training: **local funding**, paid time and a posted role that covers bills.

steps.text: Request written 2028 and 2031 staffing and paid safety terms
Save extra net pay from available school Saturday shifts
Enrol in funded local controls training only with paid time and a posted bill-covering job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger carpenters that thinking AI comes around 2031 and capable site robots around 2034. That is enough time to try a paid pilot and see what a robot really handles on a crooked stair. It isn't a promise that every carpenter gets an operator seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me more time to build a reserve and see whether the local contractor buys machines. I could lose some estimating work in 2031 and some stair hours in 2034, when I'd be about sixty-six. We have not priced retirement properly, so I cannot say I would be finished by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add forty from each paid month to the emergency reserve after the bills clear. I'd ask the trade association for a nearby controls course with a funded fee and paid study hours, and ask builders whether there is a posted operator or safety-checking role. I'd continue school and repair shifts until a real offer or actual retirement income covers the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but five years gives me a way to test the idea. I can compare an offer and our costs rather than guessing that age alone ends the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave carpentry at sixty-six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the actual pension and Lise's likely care wages cover rent, food, travel and the roof repair still owed. I would get a written estimate and set it beside twelve months of bills. If it falls short, I keep looking for paid work that my knees can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you to operate a site robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid trial on an awkward stair, a funded local course, and a posted job with enough hours and the right to stop unsafe work. I would also ask who pays for repairs to the machine. Without those terms, I would keep my saw and tape earning while they can.

say: I would use the extra time for a **paid site trial** before promising robot jobs.
I would ask for a **written retirement estimate**, not assume a finish age.
think: The longer warning gives time to build a **reserve**, but operator jobs may be scarce.
Loss of **stair hours** around 2034 could still outlast our money.
do: Add **forty** from each paid month to emergency savings after bills clear.
Ask the association about a **funded course** and builders about posted paid jobs.
Keep **site shifts** until a real offer or sufficient retirement income replaces them.
S3.quote: I can compare an offer and our costs rather than guessing that age alone ends the job.
fieldNote: David treats **retirement at sixty-six** as a calculation, not an entitlement or automatic exit.
He will compare real course funding, **posted pay** and field safety authority before leaving paid carpentry.

steps.text: Save forty from each paid month after household bills clear
Ask the trade association about funded local courses and posted roles
Keep paid site shifts until a real offer or sufficient retirement income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to watch thinking AI arrive around 2036 and robots reach site carpentry around 2039. I'd still want an actual field trial before our contractor changes the crew. Young carpenters need paid practice on real materials, not just an app lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about sixty-eight when AGI arrives, I may have enough actual retirement income to step back, but I have not checked. If the estimate is short, I'd need paid work after 2036, and the robot date in 2039 would still matter. A decade helps me plan; it does not guarantee that a Greyburn builder will hire me at seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep adding forty from paid months to the reserve while I can and request an updated retirement estimate each year. I'd teach the younger two carpenters the school stair measurements on paid site time and test any approved machine beside them. If I am still working after 2036, I'd take a posted local safety-checking role only if it pays our costs and lets me stop unsafe work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy, with more control than in the faster pictures. If the numbers support leaving before the robots, fine; if not, we need a real paid plan rather than a birthday wish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the estimate still falls short in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying for posted site or safety work I can physically do and ask the union adviser to check the income figures with Lise. I won't count an unposted robot supervisor role as wages. If neither income nor a job offer covers costs, we reduce spending and seek practical help before the reserve is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot to start a firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not with three weeks of savings now and no priced work in hand. I'd rather train the two younger carpenters on paid shifts while I can. A machine might suit a bigger firm, but it is not an investment our household can justify without real contracts and capital.

say: I would ask for **field trials** and paid practical training before robot crews replace carpenters.
I would call retirement a **real income test**, not a fixed birthday.
think: I may stop before robots only if **actual retirement income** covers our costs.
Without that, **post-2036 work** depends on a posted local role and safe knees.
do: Keep adding **forty from paid months** to the reserve after bills.
Review **retirement estimates** each year with Lise and a union adviser.
Teach two younger carpenters **stair checks** on paid shifts and test approved tools.
feel: **Uneasy**, but with time to measure the options.
S4.quote: I'd still want an actual field trial before our contractor changes the crew.
fieldNote: He enjoys testing tools and teaching **younger carpenters**, yet refuses to gamble the household on buying a robot.
His later work and retirement both depend on **actual income**, a posted local job and safe physical capacity.

steps.text: Save forty from paid months after the household bills clear
Review actual retirement estimates yearly with Lise and a union adviser
Teach two carpenters stair checks and test approved tools on paid shifts
Seek posted local safety work if income short, with manageable duties, bill-covering pay and stop authority

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest because thinking work could change in two years and robots could cut my stair wage around 2031. A funded local controls course on paid time would help only if a posted job pays enough and carries real safety authority. We also need clear staffing dates and practical help if paid site days disappear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who will teach the next carpenter to spot a bad stair. A robot can repeat a measurement, but someone must know when the old wall makes that measurement wrong. I would like the two younger workers paid to learn that before our crew changes.

headlineQuote: A robot can repeat a measurement, but someone must know when the old wall makes that measurement wrong.
portrait: David leads **school extension carpentry** and checks daily AI quantity suggestions against drawings and delivered timber.
His **low pay**, three-week reserve and Lise’s variable care shifts make an unsigned next contract serious.
He tries **approved tools** early but wants paid trials, funded local training, posted wages and safety authority.
Even in slower AGI worlds, **retirement and post-2036 work** depend on actual income and a real local opening.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives David little time before thinking work changes and site robots may cut his stair-fitting wage.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **funded local course** on paid time, a posted bill-covering role, written staffing dates and real safety authority.
